items.why: The contrast is clear, but answering only requires retrieving the explicitly negated action.
“He says” leaves the speaker unclear, and describing a message as something that “will happen” makes the question awkward.
The closing summary clearly distinguishes the group's victors from Jonathan's single kill.
Readers can identify the officer by connecting his predicted inability to eat with his death.
Following the father's requests and subsequent actions clearly identifies the rider without requiring outside knowledge.
The two covenants provide a clear contrast, though “Between whom” makes the question unnecessarily stiff.
The excerpt distinguishes Jotham's earlier governing role from his succession as king at the end.
Uzziah's sudden leprosy supplies a clear reason, distinct from the priests' effort to remove him.
The question treats the king's imagined Aramean plan as their established intention.
Readers must distinguish the men's chosen chance of survival from the two fatal options they reject.
“Who kills first” blurs the order of separate battles with the order of deaths within a battle.
The key “the news” gives no report content, such as the discovery that the camp was deserted.
The target of “Seize him!” can be identified through clear, well-supported pronoun tracking.
The passage clearly separates the priests following from the king being followed, making “him” a fair reference test.
Readers must distinguish the reporting woman's son from the quoted speaker's son to select the correct day.
The relative clause clearly identifies Zechariah, with “teaches” and “revere” providing understandable paraphrases.
The dialogue clearly separates the officer's predicted experience from the earlier announcement about food prices.
The refusal is explained, but the king's actual offer is absent; half his possessions is only hypothetical.
The final conversation is clearly placed after the meal and immediately before Paul's departure.
The order is explicit, but selecting the first action in a three-verb list is a shallow task.
Readers must distinguish the priest handing over the weapons from their former owner.
“Addressee” adds unnecessary terminology to an otherwise explicit identification of the accusers.
The purpose is explicit, but “take Amaziah's son” sounds like an unexplained physical seizure.
Readers must link “their command” to the family leaders rather than the officials who counted the troops.
Preparing the donkey for the man of God supports identifying him as the departing traveler and subsequent victim.
The officer's gate assignment makes the later “him” clear without outside story knowledge.
As punctuated, “you … and you … are all to guard” includes both sets of companies, not just the two off duty.
The letter heading lets readers distinguish the sender from the governor being addressed.
Identifying “the Philistine” requires linking Abishai's victim to the man threatening David.
The question distinguishes the men's new decision to report the discovery from their earlier looting.
Paul's request clearly separates the young informant from the prisoner sending him.
The messengers' report is clearly placed between the pursuit and the people's move into the camp.
“Whose love of soil explains the farm work” is contrived wording for a straightforward pronoun link.
The woman's “my son” and the other child's concealment clearly identify whose son was eaten.
The passage explicitly separates the king asking for prayer from the man who intercedes.
The enemy groups are explicit, but answering mainly involves reproducing a list of unfamiliar names.
The city and tomb are nested destinations, so “first” creates a fussy distinction rather than clearly separate journeys.
The stacked phrase “Ahaziah's son's nurse” creates needless kinship decoding instead of a natural question.
The passage explicitly gives Athaliah's death as the cause of calm, not the simultaneous rejoicing.
Readers must distinguish the officers receiving the order from the troops they are ordered to prepare.
The quotation separates the supposed attacking kings from the king believed to have hired them.
Matching “sending someone” to the king's earlier action clearly distinguishes the instigator from the messenger.
The quoted instruction and the following meal both identify the man of God as the intended guest.
The passage states a practical reason for the long speech, allowing one complete answer in everyday words.
Readers must distinguish the escort that turns back from the cavalry continuing with Paul.
Following “them” and “they” identifies the beaten exorcists rather than the man who attacks them.
In everyday words, both illnesses and evil spirits go away, so “leaves” unfairly demands the excerpt's exact verb.
The plan clearly distinguishes the council making the request from the commander expected to bring Paul.
“Assembling materials” obscures the scrolls and can sound like preparation for performing sorcery.
The explicit sword order names followers, but the woman is also marked for execution, making the broad question less clean.
Hearing the crowd motivates Athaliah's visit; seeing the king happens only after she arrives.
The broad “must happen” does not distinguish permission from the resulting transfer of Paul.
“Whose body is warned” is grammatically awkward and makes the body sound like the recipient of the warning.
The prophecy clearly assigns the future killing to Josiah rather than Jeroboam, who is currently at the altar.
